system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 13 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with prior Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and history of chronic cyclic nausea with dry heaves and poor solid-food tolerance was admitted to the surgical service after planned Interventional Radiology gastrostomy tube placement to transition from TPN to enteral nutrition for protein-calorie malnutrition. Post-procedure she tolerated clear liquids, then after 24 hours started tube feeds that were advanced to goal and cycled for home use, with improvement in nausea and tolerance of a regular diet as able. Pain was limited to mild tube-site discomfort controlled with oral medication; she remained afebrile and hemodynamically stable without infectious complications. She was discharged home with services on goal tube feeds and free-water flushes, with PICC removed and instructions for tube-site care and return precautions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Patel from the surgery team. I understand you came in with left upper abdominal pain. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s this sharp pain on the left, kind of under my ribs, and it shoots to my back near my shoulder blade. It’s been about a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Does anything make it worse or better—like eating, drinking, or your tube feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Eating makes it way worse. Tube feeds also bring it on, but it doesn’t last as long as when I eat by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any vomiting, fevers, chills, or black stools?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting lately. No fevers or chills. My stools have been normal, just haven’t gone in two days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I also see you’ve had a Roux-en-Y bypass and prior marginal ulcers. Have you taken any NSAIDs like ibuprofen or naproxen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I avoid them. I’m on my PPI every day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’re going to start with bowel rest—no food by mouth for now—IV fluids, pain control, and stronger acid suppression with IV pantoprazole. We’ll also check imaging to make sure there’s no perforation or obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried it’s something like a leak. Wouldn’t I be really sick?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Often people are much sicker with a leak—fever, fast heart rate, severe belly rigidity—but we don’t rely on that alone. That’s why we’re doing X-rays and checking how contrast moves through your tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your initial chest and abdominal X-rays don’t show free air, which is reassuring—no sign of a perforation on those tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why does it hurt so much when I eat?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history, an ulcer at the connection between the stomach pouch and small intestine is high on the list. We’ll likely confirm with an endoscopy—an EGD—so we can look directly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: There’s also been some drainage around my G-tube site. It’s not a lot, but it’s annoying.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll examine it closely each day. If there’s redness, pus, or worsening pain at the site, we may need to culture it, but right now the bigger issue is the pain with feeds and eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave contrast through the G-tube to check the tube position and flow. It moved through the small bowel without leaking outside the intestines, which supports that the tube is in place and there’s no extravasation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does that mean the tube isn’t causing this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It means the tube isn’t blocked and we don’t see a leak from it. It still could be that feeds irritate an ulcer or trigger pain, but it’s not malpositioned based on this study.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How was your pain overnight with no feeds and IV medications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better when I’m not eating. Still there, but not as sharp.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That pattern fits with an ulcer. We’re planning the EGD for tomorrow to confirm and guide treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had EGDs before. Are you going to fix it during the scope?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If it’s an ulcer, the main treatment is medication—high-dose acid suppression and sucralfate to coat the ulcer. We use the scope to diagnose and make sure there’s no bleeding or narrowing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re about to take you for the EGD. You’ll be sedated, and we’ll look at the gastrojejunal connection and the small bowel.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I just want to know what’s going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re back from the EGD. We found a single ulcer—about 10 millimeters—right at the gastrojejunal anastomosis. The rest looked normal, including the jejuno-jejunal connection and the limb down to the duodenal bulb.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it is an ulcer again. Is it dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be painful and can bleed if it worsens, but right now we didn’t see active bleeding or a perforation. The plan is aggressive ulcer therapy: IV pantoprazole and sucralfate, both by mouth and through the G-tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long until it stops hurting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Pain often improves over days, but healing takes longer—weeks. We’ll also adjust your nutrition so you can get calories without triggering severe pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We restarted tube feeds. You were previously cycling at a higher rate. How did it feel at the cycled rate?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: At the higher rate it was awful—cramping and that same left-sided pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to switch from cycling to continuous feeds at a lower rate—55 mL per hour—to reduce the stress on the anastomosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s a little better at the slower rate, but I still feel pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understood. If it persists, we can try a more concentrated formula at an even lower rate so the volume is smaller.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We changed to a concentrated formula at 30 mL per hour. Any change?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still hurts. Not as intense as eating, but it’s there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep the ulcer meds going and also advance your oral diet carefully to a bariatric stage 5 diet—small, soft meals—only as tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I tried a little food and it flared up again. I’m scared to eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. For now, don’t push through severe pain. We’ll prioritize healing and nutrition, and we’ll keep portions very small and bland when you do try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs look stable—white count is normal, kidney function is normal. Hemoglobin is a bit low, but not dropping, which argues against active bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could the pain be from constipation? I haven’t gone much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Constipation can add discomfort. We’ll start stool softener and a stimulant laxative as needed. But the meal-related sharp pain pattern still points to the ulcer as the main driver.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We obtained a CT scan of your abdomen and pelvis with contrast. It shows no bowel obstruction and no gastrogastric fistula. It does show a large stool burden in the rectum, so constipation is definitely part of the picture.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s a fistula?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: After bypass, a fistula would be an abnormal connection between the small stomach pouch and the larger remnant stomach. It can cause ulcers and symptoms. Your CT did not show that, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: There’s a little bump above my belly button that’s tender.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We see a small pustule there. We’re going to open it at the bedside to drain it and send a culture, to make sure there’s no spreading skin infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That drainage was gross. Is it serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was small and localized. You’re afebrile and your vitals are stable, which is reassuring. We’ll keep it clean and watch for redness spreading. The culture will tell us what bacteria it is.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because you’re still having significant pain with tube feeds and you need reliable nutrition, we’re going to start TPN—nutrition through the vein. That requires a PICC line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had a PICC before. Are there risks?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—clot, infection, and line malposition. We place it with sterile technique and confirm position with a chest X-ray. We’ll remove it as soon as we can get you back to tube feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your first chest X-ray shows the PICC tip was bent back a bit in the upper central vein. The PICC nurse is going to adjust it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Repeat X-ray looks good now—the PICC tip is in the low SVC where we want it. We can safely use it for TPN.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no tube feeds at all right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. We’re stopping tube feeds for now to let the ulcer calm down and to avoid triggering pain. You’ll get calories, protein, vitamins, and fluids through TPN while we continue the ulcer medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How is your pain today compared to when feeds were running?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s better. Still sore, but I’m not getting those spikes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s encouraging. We’ll keep you on IV pantoprazole and sucralfate. The goal is to transition back to enteral feeds once you can tolerate them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do we need to move the G-tube? It feels like it’s part of the problem.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We discussed it with Interventional Radiology. Because your gastric remnant is small, they don’t think repositioning is feasible. Another option is converting to a GJ tube that feeds into the jejunum, but that’s a different tube and procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want another tube procedure if I can avoid it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s reasonable. We’ll keep it as a backup option if we can’t find a feeding plan you can tolerate through the current tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your skin culture from the pustule grew Staph aureus that is resistant to oxacillin, which means MRSA. The good news is it’s localized and you’ve had no fevers or spreading redness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: MRSA sounds scary. Am I contagious? Is it in my blood?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a common skin bacteria that can be resistant to some antibiotics. Right now it’s from the abscess drainage, not your blood. We’ll focus on local wound care and monitoring. If you develop fever, worsening redness, or new drainage, tell us right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When can I go home? I hate being on TPN.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We want you home too, but only once we have a nutrition plan that doesn’t cause severe pain. The plan is to retrial tube feeds once the ulcer pain is more controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today we’re going to retrial tube feeds. We’ll stop TPN once we see you can tolerate feeds again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous it’ll hurt like before, especially at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start cautiously and adjust the regimen based on your symptoms. If pain increases, we can change the formula or rate rather than pushing through.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s worse at night again. During the day it’s tolerable, but now it’s really bothering me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for telling us. We’re going to switch to a more easily absorbed, ‘pre-digested’ bariatric formula—Peptamen Bariatric—to improve tolerance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How did you do overnight after switching to Peptamen Bariatric?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I still feel some discomfort, but it’s not that stabbing pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’re going to trial cycling it at 60 mL per hour for 12 hours, with water flushes every 4 hours and before/after meds. If you tolerate that, we can stop TPN and remove the PICC.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If I go home on this, what meds do I need to keep taking?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Two key ulcer meds: liquid pantoprazole 40 mg twice a day, and sucralfate four times a day—both by mouth and through the G-tube as instructed. And absolutely no NSAIDs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my constipation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home with docusate twice daily and senna as needed. Keep up fluids and walking. If you go several days without a bowel movement or have worsening pain, call.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I heard pain service changed my nortriptyline. I’m confused—do I take 25 or 50?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You should take 50 mg at bedtime now and stop the 25 mg tablets. Please notify your prescribing doctor and therapist about the change as soon as you can.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve stopped TPN and removed the PICC today since you’re tolerating the tube feeds. Your vital signs are stable and you’re walking independently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should make me come back to the ER?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Come back for vomiting where you can’t keep fluids or meds down, signs of dehydration like dizziness, any black or bloody stools or vomit, fever or chills, worsening or changing abdominal pain, chest pain, or shortness of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the G-tube site—can I shower? What if it drains?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can wash around it with mild soap and water. If there’s no drainage, you don’t need a dressing. If you see increasing redness, pus, foul smell, or worsening pain, call us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need to check anything before I start feeds at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—aspirate the tube with a 60 mL syringe before feeding to check residual. If you pull back more than 50 mL, stop the feeding and notify the clinician managing your feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When do I follow up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Follow up with your surgeon in about a week, and with Gastroenterology in about three weeks. We’ll also arrange home services to help with tube feeding supplies and support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go—any last questions about the ulcer treatment or the feeding plan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just… will this ulcer keep coming back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Some people do get recurrent marginal ulcers after bypass. Staying on the PPI as prescribed, taking sucralfate, avoiding NSAIDs, and following the bariatric diet guidance lowers the risk. If pain returns, call early so we can address it before it escalates.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m relieved we found an answer. Thank you.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with prior Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and gastrostomy tube for nutritional supplementation was admitted to the surgical service with one week of sharp left upper quadrant pain radiating to the back and worsened by oral intake and tube feeds. Initial evaluation included chest/abdominal radiographs and contrast assessment via G-tube without evidence of free air or extravasation. On hospital day 2, EGD demonstrated a single 10 mm gastrojejunal anastomotic ulcer with otherwise normal post-bypass anatomy. She was treated with IV pantoprazole and sucralfate (oral and via G-tube) and underwent multiple tube-feeding adjustments due to pain intolerance; ultimately tube feeds were held and TPN was started via PICC (with radiographic confirmation of line position). CT abdomen/pelvis showed no obstruction or gastrogastric fistula but did note significant stool burden. A small supraumbilical pustule was drained and cultured, growing MRSA without systemic infection. Tube feeds were retrialed late in the course; TPN was discontinued and the PICC removed after improved tolerance on Peptamen Bariatric cycled at 60 mL/hr for 12 hours with scheduled water flushes. She was discharged home with services on liquid pantoprazole BID, sucralfate QID (oral and via G-tube), bowel regimen, pain control plan including increased bedtime nortriptyline, and close surgical and GI follow-up.

conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep the ulcer meds going and also advance your oral diet carefully to a bariatric stage 5 diet—small, soft meals—only as tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I tried a little food and it flared up again. I’m scared to eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. For now, don’t push through severe pain. We’ll prioritize healing and nutrition, and we’ll keep portions very small and bland when you do try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs look stable—white count is normal, kidney function is normal. Hemoglobin is a bit low, but not dropping, which argues against active bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could the pain be from constipation? I haven’t gone much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Constipation can add discomfort. We’ll start stool softener and a stimulant laxative as needed. But the meal-related sharp pain pattern still points to the ulcer as the main driver.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We obtained a CT scan of your abdomen and pelvis with contrast. It shows no bowel obstruction and no gastrogastric fistula. It does show a large stool burden in the rectum, so constipation is definitely part of the picture.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s a fistula?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: After bypass, a fistula would be an abnormal connection between the small stomach pouch and the larger remnant stomach. It can cause ulcers and symptoms. Your CT did not show that, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: There’s a little bump above my belly button that’s tender.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We see a small pustule there. We’re going to open it at the bedside to drain it and send a culture, to make sure there’s no spreading skin infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That drainage was gross. Is it serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was small and localized. You’re afebrile and your vitals are stable, which is reassuring. We’ll keep it clean and watch for redness spreading. The culture will tell us what bacteria it is.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because you’re still having significant pain with tube feeds and you need reliable nutrition, we’re going to start TPN—nutrition through the vein. That requires a PICC line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had a PICC before. Are there risks?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—clot, infection, and line malposition. We place it with sterile technique and confirm position with a chest X-ray. We’ll remove it as soon as we can get you back to tube feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your first chest X-ray shows the PICC tip was bent back a bit in the upper central vein. The PICC nurse is going to adjust it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Repeat X-ray looks good now—the PICC tip is in the low SVC where we want it. We can safely use it for TPN.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no tube feeds at all right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. We’re stopping tube feeds for now to let the ulcer calm down and to avoid triggering pain. You’ll get calories, protein, vitamins, and fluids through TPN while we continue the ulcer medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How is your pain today compared to when feeds were running?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s better. Still sore, but I’m not getting those spikes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s encouraging. We’ll keep you on IV pantoprazole and sucralfate. The goal is to transition back to enteral feeds once you can tolerate them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do we need to move the G-tube? It feels like it’s part of the problem.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We discussed it with Interventional Radiology. Because your gastric remnant is small, they don’t think repositioning is feasible. Another option is converting to a GJ tube that feeds into the jejunum, but that’s a different tube and procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want another tube procedure if I can avoid it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s reasonable. We’ll keep it as a backup option if we can’t find a feeding plan you can tolerate through the current tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your skin culture from the pustule grew Staph aureus that is resistant to oxacillin, which means MRSA. The good news is it’s localized and you’ve had no fevers or spreading redness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: MRSA sounds scary. Am I contagious? Is it in my blood?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a common skin bacteria that can be resistant to some antibiotics. Right now it’s from the abscess drainage, not your blood. We’ll focus on local wound care and monitoring. If you develop fever, worsening redness, or new drainage, tell us right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When can I go home? I hate being on TPN.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We want you home too, but only once we have a nutrition plan that doesn’t cause severe pain. The plan is to retrial tube feeds once the ulcer pain is more controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today we’re going to retrial tube feeds. We’ll stop TPN once we see you can tolerate feeds again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous it’ll hurt like before, especially at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start cautiously and adjust the regimen based on your symptoms. If pain increases, we can change the formula or rate rather than pushing through.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s worse at night again. During the day it’s tolerable, but now it’s really bothering me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for telling us. We’re going to switch to a more easily absorbed, ‘pre-digested’ bariatric formula—Peptamen Bariatric—to improve tolerance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How did you do overnight after switching to Peptamen Bariatric?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I still feel some discomfort, but it’s not that stabbing pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’re going to trial cycling it at 60 mL per hour for 12 hours, with water flushes every 4 hours and before/after meds. If you tolerate that, we can stop TPN and remove the PICC.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If I go home on this, what meds do I need to keep taking?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Two key ulcer meds: liquid pantoprazole 40 mg twice a day, and sucralfate four times a day—both by mouth and through the G-tube as instructed. And absolutely no NSAIDs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my constipation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home with docusate twice daily and senna as needed. Keep up fluids and walking. If you go several days without a bowel movement or have worsening pain, call.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I heard pain service changed my nortriptyline. I’m confused—do I take 25 or 50?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You should take 50 mg at bedtime now and stop the 25 mg tablets. Please notify your prescribing doctor and therapist about the change as soon as you can.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve stopped TPN and removed the PICC today since you’re tolerating the tube feeds. Your vital signs are stable and you’re walking independently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should make me come back to the ER?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Come back for vomiting where you can’t keep fluids or meds down, signs of dehydration like dizziness, any black or bloody stools or vomit, fever or chills, worsening or changing abdominal pain, chest pain, or shortness of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the G-tube site—can I shower? What if it drains?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can wash around it with mild soap and water. If there’s no drainage, you don’t need a dressing. If you see increasing redness, pus, foul smell, or worsening pain, call us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need to check anything before I start feeds at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—aspirate the tube with a 60 mL syringe before feeding to check residual. If you pull back more than 50 mL, stop the feeding and notify the clinician managing your feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When do I follow up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Follow up with your surgeon in about a week, and with Gastroenterology in about three weeks. We’ll also arrange home services to help with tube feeding supplies and support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go—any last questions about the ulcer treatment or the feeding plan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just… will this ulcer keep coming back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Some people do get recurrent marginal ulcers after bypass. Staying on the PPI as prescribed, taking sucralfate, avoiding NSAIDs, and following the bariatric diet guidance lowers the risk. If pain returns, call early so we can address it before it escalates.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m relieved we found an answer. Thank you.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with prior Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and gastrostomy tube for nutritional supplementation was admitted to the surgical service with one week of sharp left upper quadrant pain radiating to the back and worsened by oral intake and tube feeds. Initial evaluation included chest/abdominal radiographs and contrast assessment via G-tube without evidence of free air or extravasation. On hospital day 2, EGD demonstrated a single 10 mm gastrojejunal anastomotic ulcer with otherwise normal post-bypass anatomy. She was treated with IV pantoprazole and sucralfate (oral and via G-tube) and underwent multiple tube-feeding adjustments due to pain intolerance; ultimately tube feeds were held and TPN was started via PICC (with radiographic confirmation of line position). CT abdomen/pelvis showed no obstruction or gastrogastric fistula but did note significant stool burden. A small supraumbilical pustule was drained and cultured, growing MRSA without systemic infection. Tube feeds were retrialed late in the course; TPN was discontinued and the PICC removed after improved tolerance on Peptamen Bariatric cycled at 60 mL/hr for 12 hours with scheduled water flushes. She was discharged home with services on liquid pantoprazole BID, sucralfate QID (oral and via G-tube), bowel regimen, pain control plan including increased bedtime nortriptyline, and close surgical and GI follow-up.
